hints: Compare the three descriptions carefully - focus on nucleus shape (bean-shaped vs large spherical vs lobed) and the clue about function.
Remember which agranulocyte leaves the blood to develop into a large tissue phagocyte, and which agranulocyte with very little cytoplasm is responsible for responding to antigens.
Recall the most abundant granulocyte with a multi-lobed nucleus that carries out phagocytosis in the blood.
walkthrough:
Link Nucleus Shape to Cell Type**
Think of what you would see under the microscope. A large cell with a kidney or bean-shaped nucleus that can leave the blood and grow into a macrophage in tissues is the monocyte. It is an agranulocyte specialised for later phagocytosis outside the blood.

Link Large Round Nucleus to Specific Response**
A cell almost filled by a large spherical nucleus with only a thin rim of cytoplasm is the lymphocyte. It does not carry out phagocytosis but recognises non-self antigens to give a specific immune response by making antibodies or killing infected cells.

Link Lobed Nucleus to Phagocytosis in Blood**
A cell with a lobed, multi-part nucleus that is phagocytic in the blood is the neutrophil. It is a granulocyte and the first phagocyte to engulf pathogens.

Final answer: Bean-shaped nucleus developing into macrophage - monocyte; large spherical nucleus with little cytoplasm responding to non-self antigens - lymphocyte; lobed nucleus and phagocytic - neutrophil.

hints: Start from the problem in the stem - loss of up to 30% body mass as water makes plasma volume fall, so blood becomes thicker and harder to push through capillaries.
Compare Fig. 2.1 with Fig. 2.2 at the same magnification - look at shape (oval vs round biconcave disc) and relative size and number of cells in the field of view.
Link smaller, streamlined cells present in larger numbers to easier flow and maintained transport when blood is viscous.
walkthrough:
State the Functional Advantage**
When dehydrated, less water in plasma means thicker, more viscous blood. If red cells can still slip past each other and through narrow capillaries, circulation and oxygen delivery can continue. That is the key adaptation to state first.

Describe the Structural Differences**
At $\times 2000$ the camel cells in Fig. 2.1 are small, oval or lozenge-shaped, almost torpedo-like, while human cells in Fig. 2.2 are larger round biconcave discs. Because they are smaller, more camel cells fit into the same field of view, meaning more cells per unit volume.

Link Structure to Flow**
A small streamlined elliptical shape offers less resistance and aligns more easily with flow, so viscous blood keeps moving. Smaller size plus higher number helps maintain total surface area and oxygen transport even when plasma is reduced.

Final answer: Allows easier / quicker flow / movement of blood despite increased viscosity; camel cells are lozenge / elliptical / torpedo-shaped vs human biconcave discs; camel cells are smaller than human cells; larger number of camel cells per unit volume.

hints: Read the graph at the lung value given in the stem - find $6.4 \text{ kPa}$ on the x-axis and read across to both curves, then across to % saturation.
Decide which curve lies to the left at that partial pressure and remember what left-shift means for loading oxygen in the lungs.
Link higher saturation in the lungs to the consequence for transport and release in tissues at low environmental oxygen.
walkthrough:
Extract Paired Data at Lung $pO_2$**
Find $6.4 \text{ kPa}$ (lungs at $3500 \text{ m}$) on the x-axis. Move up to the solid llama curve then across: about $86$% saturated. Move up to the dashed human curve then across: about $79$-$80$% saturated. Always quote both values with units to show comparison.

Interpret as Affinity Difference**
Over the low $pO_2$ range the llama curve lies to the left of the human curve. Left means at any given $pO_2$ haemoglobin picks up more oxygen, so llama haemoglobin has higher affinity for oxygen. That is ideal where air pressure and $pO_2$ are low.

Explain the Adaptive Benefit**
Higher saturation in the lungs means each unit of blood leaves with more oxygen bound. More oxygen can then be transported and unloaded in tissues, helping maintain aerobic respiration despite thin air.

Final answer: Llama haemoglobin is more saturated than human at high altitude lung $pO_2$; at $6.4 \text{ kPa}$ llama ~86% saturated vs human ~79-80%; llama haemoglobin has higher affinity for oxygen (curve to left); so more oxygen taken up in lungs and transported / delivered to tissues to meet demand.

hints: Recall that increased carbon dioxide lowers haemoglobin affinity, so for the same $pO_2$ saturation is lower - think which side of the original human curve that new curve must lie on.
walkthrough:
Apply the Right Shift**
More carbon dioxide reduces affinity, so haemoglobin holds less oxygen at any $pO_2$. Sketch a sigmoid curve of similar shape but shifted right and slightly down from the dashed human curve, showing lower percentage saturation.
Final answer: New human curve drawn to the right of / below the original adult human curve (same sigmoid shape, lower % saturation at each $pO_2$).

hints: Start with what a metabolically active organ like the liver produces in large amounts during respiration.
Think how that product changes the blood chemistry around haemoglobin and what that does to haemoglobin affinity for oxygen.
Link the change in affinity to the benefit for an organ with a high demand for ATP.
walkthrough:
High $CO_2$ Where Respiration is Fast**
Liver cells respiring rapidly release a lot of carbon dioxide, so $pCO_2$ in the capillaries is high. Carbon dioxide combines with water and affects haemoglobin, forming haemoglobinic acid and releasing $H^+$ ions.

Lower Affinity Means Unloading**
$H^+$ and $CO_2$ lower the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen. This is the Bohr shift - the dissociation curve moves right. Haemoglobin therefore releases its oxygen more readily exactly where $CO_2$ is highest.

Match Supply to Demand**
More oxygen diffuses to the active cells, allowing more aerobic respiration and more ATP synthesis to support metabolic work. In short, the waste product of respiration promotes delivery of more oxygen for further respiration.

Final answer: Active organs release more carbon dioxide / have higher $pCO_2$; this decreases haemoglobin affinity for oxygen e.g. formation of haemoglobinic acid / H+ effect (Bohr shift); more oxygen released / unloaded; for more aerobic respiration / ATP production.
